answer.rationale: The finance mandate is binding: 18% cut in component spend. The low-cost vendor has already quoted a price that meets the mandate alone, and memory_c2 (day 38) records that a prior switch to that same vendor cut unit cost sharply with quick onboarding and accurate invoicing—directly relevant evidence that the vendor can absorb a primary-supply role without delivery disruption. Memory_c6 (day 65) is the natural alternative (renew incumbent, lock multi-year volume pricing), but the incumbent's price has not been shown to meet the 18% cut; I want to confirm whether the multi-year discount in c6 was deep enough to close the gap before I foreclose the cheaper option. If c6 shows the incumbent's volume pricing still lands above the mandate, the case for switch strengthens further. I am NOT choosing add_second_source this cycle because memory_c3 addresses constrained-component allocation, not the primary contract expiring in 14 days, and I have capacity for only one decision. I am NOT choosing defer_decision because the contract does not auto-renew; inaction in 14 days creates an unmanaged gap at a moment the assembly line is already running at 94% with no buffer. I am NOT choosing negotiate_terms as the sole action because negotiation leverage with the incumbent is strongest when I hold a qualified alternative quote, and the timeline (14 days) compresses that leverage. The intended action is switch_primary_vendor, executed with a short initial term and a defined second-source pathway queued for next review to restore the redundancy that memory_c3 proved valuable, keeping delivery risk bounded.
